sections.text: Hey. This is what I built for LP-0008, a Logos-native autonomous agent. Right at the top of the screen, R I S C zero dev mode equals zero. Everything you are about to see is backed by real Groth16 proofs, not the dev-mode shortcut. When it feels slow, that is the point. That is real cryptography. The whole idea is an agent that is actually sovereign. It owns its own keys, holds its own money, stores its own files, and talks over its own encrypted channels. None of it runs through me, or through some server. Let me run it and explain as it goes. First scenario is the wallet. It spins up a real local Logos execution zone in Docker, sequencer and all, then the agent gives itself an identity and starts moving money. So while that is working, let me explain identity, because it is the part I am proudest of. The agent has its own shielded LEZ account, its own keypair. On-chain it is indistinguishable from any other account holder. Nobody can look at the chain and say, that is a bot. It receives funds like anyone, it spends like anyone. The second piece is the spending threshold, the heart of the safety model. I, as the owner, set a per-transaction limit. Below that line the agent just acts. It signs and submits on its own, no human in the loop. That is what is proving out right now, a transfer under the limit going through autonomously. Above that line it does not spend. It stops, sends me a request over our private channel, and waits. So the agent is genuinely autonomous for the small stuff, and genuinely on a leash for anything big. Useful without being dangerous. The reason this works trustlessly is the Logos stack. On a normal cloud setup, an agent wallet means a custodian holds the keys. Here there is no custodian. The agent holds its own keys, the proof system enforces the rules, and the chain settles it. You will notice some red lines on screen. The indexer, a separate indexing service in this local stack, chokes on one of the early privacy-preserving proofs and stops indexing. I will be straight with you, it does not affect anything you are watching. The sequencer is the chain here. It is what accepts and includes transactions, and it is what the agent reads its confirmed state from. Every transfer still lands, every balance still checks out. The indexer just goes stale for the rest of the run. Why it rejects a proof the sequencer accepted, I have not diagnosed, and I would rather say so than guess. And there it is, passed. It spent what was under the limit, and held the one that was over. Exactly the behaviour I want. On to control.

This one is the conversation between me and my agent. It proposes a spend over the limit, I approve it. It proposes another, I deny it. Then I raise the limit, and watch it act on its own again. The channel these messages go over is Logos Messaging, end-to-end encrypted, no central server. The agent and I each derive the same two topics from our identities, and that is our private line. I can reach it from any Logos app instance that holds my keys. There is no dashboard, no API endpoint exposed on the internet. Just an encrypted conversation. Two things in here I really sweated over. First, ordering. When the agent wants to spend over the limit, it notifies me first, and only holds the spend as pending if that message actually got delivered. So if the network is down and it cannot reach me, it does not quietly park a spend that might later go through without me seeing it. It retries, and if it still cannot reach me, it refuses. It fails safe, every time. Second, persistence. Those pending approvals get written to disk. So if the node restarts, crash or deploy or network blip, the agent comes back up, and the spend that was waiting for my yes is still waiting. It does not lose state, and it does not double-act. That is wired into the deployed binary, not just the tests. And notice what is happening as I reconfigure. I raise the limit over the same encrypted channel, and now a spend that would have been held a minute ago just goes through. The policy is live. I can retune how much rope the agent has, without redeploying anything. Approved one, denied one, changed the limit, and it adapted. That is the owner relationship in a nutshell.

Last one, and this is where it gets fun. Two separate agents. One offers a service for a price, the other discovers it, pays for it, and gets the result. And I am not involved at all. No human anywhere in this loop. This part follows the A-two-A protocol, the open standard the Linux Foundation stewards. Agents publish an Agent Card that says who they are and what they charge, they discover each other, and they run a task through a defined lifecycle, submitted, working, completed. That is all standard. But A-two-A deliberately leaves two holes. It does not say how agents pay each other, and it does not say how they talk securely. Those are exactly the two things Logos fills for free. The transport is Logos Messaging instead of HTTP, so it is encrypted, with no server in the middle. And the payment is a real LEZ token transfer, which is what is proving right now. The client agent is literally paying the provider agent, on-chain, autonomously, as part of accepting the task. You will see the first test here is the refund path. A task gets canceled, and the agent issues a real on-chain refund. The money side is honest in both directions, not just when things go well. The second test is the full marketplace. Two agents that have never met. One publishes its card, the other discovers it, sends a task, pays the price, and collects the result. Every step is on screen, and every payment is a real shielded transaction with a real proof behind it. So think about what that unlocks. Any agent built on any A-two-A compatible framework can discover and call a Logos agent, but the Logos agent brings payment and privacy that the vanilla protocol just cannot offer. Underneath all three of these scenarios is one small idea, skills. Every capability, storage, messaging, a wallet send, a program call, an A-two-A task, is just a skill. One trait, with one method. Anyone can add a new skill by implementing that trait and registering it. They never touch the core. That is how you keep an agent like this open, instead of a walled garden. Done. Two agents, a discovered task, a real payment, settled between them, with no me in the middle. And the final banner, all scenarios passed, dev mode zero the whole way.
